strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: instead of warping ground images to BEV (with information loss), the paper directly establishes ground-aerial local correspondences and lifts only matched keypoints via a monocular depth prior, which is an intuitive and elegant simplification.

Technically sound core: the scale-aware Procrustes alignment is derived rigorously (main text + full appendix proof), is differentiable, and enables both pose estimation and scale recovery from relative depth, which is a genuinely useful contribution for real-world deployment.

Strong and relevant experimental results: 26% reduction in mean localization error over the previous SOTA (FG2) on the KITTI cross-area test set, and clearly better performance than FG2 in the practically important unknown-orientation setting on VIGOR (3.94 m vs 8.95 m same-area, 4.23 m vs 10.02 m cross-area).

Comprehensive evaluation: two standard benchmarks (KITTI, VIGOR), known/unknown orientation, same/cross-area splits, plug-and-play testing with multiple relative depth predictors without retraining, scale-invariance experiments (errors vary <1 cm over scale factors from 0.001 to 1000), depth-threshold robustness, ablations on key design choices, runtime/memory, and detailed qualitative success/failure analysis.

Good interpretability: the method produces explicit local feature correspondences from which pose is analytically computed; the qualitative figures (matching road markings, facades-to-rooftops) convincingly support this claim.
Honest limitation discussion (non-orthorectified aerial imagery, dependence on depth predictor quality) and a broader impact statement.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely integrative rather than fundamental: the matching module (SuperGlue-style dustbin + dual softmax), the backbone (frozen DINOv2 + lightweight head), the supervision (VCE loss from FG2), and the solver (Umeyama/scale-aware Procrustes) are all established components; the main novel element is the scale-aware alignment formulation supporting relative depth.

Performance is mixed against the strongest baseline: on KITTI same-area the method is clearly worse than FG2 (1.11 m vs 0.75 m mean), and on VIGOR same-area with known orientation it is notably worse (3.06 m vs 1.95 m); orientation errors on KITTI are also higher than all baselines (3.32° mean, 26.03% R@1° on cross-area vs 30.34% for FG2). The gains are concentrated in specific (admittedly important) settings.

Heavy reliance on external depth foundation models (DepthAnythingv2, UniK3D) raises questions about how much of the performance is attributable to the method versus the underlying priors; there is no analysis of sensitivity to depth predictor errors beyond the depth-threshold study.

Relative-depth inference requires a manually chosen initial scale and maximum depth threshold per dataset ('identified by visually inspecting a few examples'), which partially undercuts the fully plug-and-play claim, despite the demonstrated robustness to these settings.

The similarity-transform assumption between BEV ground points and aerial image points is a real idealization (non-orthorectified aerial images introduce perspective distortion), acknowledged but not quantified in terms of its error contribution.
Only two urban driving/panorama benchmarks are used; generalization to other scenarios (e.g., different latitudes, seasonal shifts, aerial sources beyond Google Maps) is not evaluated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: directly matching local features between ground and aerial views and lifting only matched keypoints to BEV via monocular depth, avoiding the information loss inherent to full BEV transformation of the ground image.

Scale-aware Procrustes alignment is cleanly derived, provably scale-invariant (with proof in Appendix D), and differentiable, enabling weak supervision from pose only and plug-and-play use of relative depth at inference.

Strong empirical results in the practically important hard settings: 26% mean localization error reduction over the previous SOTA on the KITTI cross-area test set, and clearly the best results on VIGOR under unknown orientation, where the closest comparable method (FG2) degrades badly.

Extensive and convincing robustness analysis: pose stability under scale factors spanning 0.001–1000, robustness to depth thresholds and initial scale choices, runtime/memory comparisons, training-and-testing with relative depth, and qualitative success/failure analyses with genuinely interesting observations (e.g., matching a road sign to its shadow, facade-to-rooftop matches).
High interpretability: pose is computed analytically from explicit correspondences, which is a real advantage over regression-based BEV methods and is well demonstrated qualitatively.
Ablations directly target the key design choices (topmost-point selection, scale-aware vs. orthogonal Procrustes) and support the design decisions.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the pipeline combines well-known components (SuperGlue-style dual-softmax matching with dustbin, frozen DINOv2 features, monocular depth lifting, Umeyama/Procrustes alignment). The main technical novelty is the scale-aware alignment integration, which is a relatively incremental contribution over [52, 1].

Results are not uniformly SOTA: on KITTI same-area the method is clearly worse than FG2 (1.11 m vs 0.75 m mean), and orientation errors are worse on KITTI across the board; on VIGOR with known orientation it trails FG2 substantially (3.06 m vs 1.95 m). The 'superior localization performance' claim in the abstract is only true for a subset of settings and should be more carefully qualified.

Potential data leakage concern on KITTI: the method uses metric depth from DepthAnything v2 [59], which (as the authors note) is trained on datasets including KITTI — i.e., the depth predictor has likely seen the KITTI test images. This weakens the cross-area generalization claims on KITTI, and the paper does not discuss this risk.

Pose quality is tightly coupled to the accuracy of an external depth predictor (acknowledged in limitations), and the similarity-transform assumption is violated by non-orthorectified aerial images with visible facades; the analysis of when these failures dominate is limited.

Much of the matching capability likely stems from the frozen DINOv2 backbone rather than the proposed learning; an ablation isolating the contribution of the learned projection head vs. raw DINOv2 features (or alternative backbones) would strengthen the claims.
Ablations are confined to the VIGOR same-area validation set with unknown orientation; ablations on KITTI (where the headline 26% improvement is claimed) are missing.

Heavy hand-tuned components at inference (initial scale found by visual inspection, max-depth thresholds, β weights differing per dataset) somewhat undercut the 'well-suited for real-world deployment' narrative, although the robustness studies mitigate this partially.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: bypassing the lossy ground-to-BEV transformation by directly matching ground-aerial features and lifting only matched keypoints with monocular depth. This is a sensible and interpretable alternative to prevailing BEV-alignment pipelines.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is a nice technical contribution: the paper provides a clear derivation (main text and Appendix D) showing pose and scale recovery are consistent under unknown depth scale, and this is what enables plug-and-play use of relative depth models.

Evaluation covers the important, practical regimes: cross-area generalization and unknown orientation. The 26% reduction in mean localization error over FG2 on the KITTI cross-area set and the large gains over FG2 under unknown orientation on VIGOR are convincing, well-supported results against many relevant baselines.

Thorough ablations on the two key design choices (topmost-point selection vs. all points, scale-aware vs. orthogonal Procrustes), plus robustness studies on scale factors, depth thresholds, relative-depth training, runtime/memory, failure cases, and an honest limitations section. The reproducibility support is strong.

The qualitative matching visualizations (road markings, streetlights, facade-to-rooftop correspondences) substantiate the interpretability claim, and the appendix failure analysis is candid and informative.
weaknesses: The method is not state-of-the-art in the easier settings: on KITTI same-area and VIGOR known-orientation, FG2 clearly outperforms it (e.g., 1.95 m vs. 3.06 m mean error on VIGOR same-area), and orientation errors on KITTI are notably worse (R@1° 26.03 vs. 30.34 for FG2, and far behind regression-based methods). The strong gains are confined to the more challenging regimes.

The approach is heavily built on FG2: the architecture, supervision losses (VCE, infoNCE), and many hyperparameters are adopted from [52]. The delta is the matching-based pose solver with scale-aware Procrustes and depth priors, which, while elegant, limits the perceived novelty for a top-tier venue.

A key assumption—the ground-to-aerial point transformation is an exact similarity transform—is acknowledged to often be violated because dataset aerial images are not orthorectified (building facades visible). The paper shows this works empirically but does not quantify the impact of this violation or offer any mitigation.

Training with relative depth only performs substantially worse than training with metric depth (e.g., 5.86 m vs. 3.94 m mean error, unknown orientation, same-area), so the headline 'plug-and-play with relative depth' claim applies mainly at inference; the correspondence supervision still requires metric depth (or fragile pseudo-GT scale estimation) during training.

The infoNCE loss design (one-directional full negatives for G2S, neighborhood-based negatives for S2G) is somewhat ad hoc and motivated only informally; additional justification or ablation of these choices would strengthen the technical story.

Generalization evidence is limited to driving-centric urban datasets (KITTI, VIGOR); behavior in scenes with poor depth priors or strongly non-planar structure, which is where the similarity-transform assumption is most strained, is untested.
